account:
Today I have been following my appointments, though the afternoon has slipped badly. I am now at the east-bank cottage for tea with the neighbour, who is waiting; freight is here too. I have not yet heard what either wants to discuss. Earlier I visited the mill for the scheduled grain inspection. I saw hay stocked at its stall, but that alone tells me nothing unusual.

The main unresolved business concerns talk of changes to the bridge or port. Yesterday the innkeeper denied proposing or announcing such changes and traced the matter only to a vague rumour from Townsfolk 03. The builder reported the bridge passable, and relayed freight's account of undamaged roads and an uneventful ferry crossing. None of that establishes a proposal or a need for repairs. Today the builder delivered a signed Bridge and Landing Survey to the secretary. I heard him say no specific defects were observed; the secretary said the crossings worked but the report was not structural certification. I have paid the agreed two emeralds, but have not read the report myself. The secretary mistakenly handed me my appointment book instead, which I returned. That mix-up and the difficulty exchanging the report have delayed matters, but I have no evidence they were deliberate.

No council letters had been handed to the secretary for my one-o'clock appointment. That is missing correspondence, not proof that anyone is concealing it. The baker has been selling bread at the market, with a fresh-stock announcement from Townsfolk 28; I also heard distant speech from the baker but could not understand it. I cannot infer its subject.

I suspect there may be discussion about the crossings or waterfront that has not reached me, but I do not yet know of an organized plan, its participants, or its purpose. A transport or trading concern is possible, given the rumour's subject, but remains speculation. Tea offers a chance to ask the neighbour and freight what they have actually seen or heard. I should distinguish firsthand information from rumour, then obtain and read the survey when I return to the office.
